catalog_quote: 3. Tone 3.1. Bassa is a discrete level tone language.[fn 4] Hobley(1964) identified three tonemes (high, mid and low), but she noted that there were two groups of low tones. One group of low tones rises before a following low tone and the other group of low tones does not. I would like to propose that the group of low tones which rises before a following low is actually an underlying low-mid tone. Illustrations of these four tonemes on CV words are: [Table 5. Tones on CV words ...] Low tone does not occur on CV nouns. [fn 4, p. 49] In this paper I follow Wm. E. Welmers' classification of tone languages. He defines a discrete level tone language as one which as [sic] "two, three or four level tones, and perhaps also a unit rising and/or a unit falling tone". In discrete level tone languages the position of the glides within the environmental pitch range is not significant. [Hobley 1964: 51] Bassa is a register-tone language with a slight overlap of contour-tone characteristics. ... Bassa has three registers, high, mid, and low. Tonemes usually appear on vowels, but they can also appear on syllabic nasals. [Vogler 2017: 7] Les systèmes de tons sont à trois (bassa, klao, neyo...) ou quatre registres (grebo, bété, vata...).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bassa is described purely as a level-tone language (four tonemes H, M, L, LM in Bertkau; three registers H, M, L in Hobley), every syllable/vowel (and syllabic nasal) bearing lexical tone; neither description posits word stress or accent, and no statement about stress placement, its absence, or its non-contrastiveness is made anywhere in the accessible descriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The only occurrences of 'stress' in Bertkau 1975 (ch. 5, pp. 39-42) concern the stress of English source words determining the tone melody of loanwords (e.g. initial-stressed disyllables > CV́CV̀), i.e. English stress is mapped onto Bassa high tone, which is indirect evidence that Bassa itself has no stress category in the author's analysis but is not stated as such.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described on CV/CVV words and in frames (word and phrase level); intonation chapter covers only yes-no question marking by an added final low-toned vowel. No word-stress domain discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Bertkau 1975 describes central (Grand Bassa County, Buchanan-area) Bassa, noting that the eastern Gbi-Doru dialects (Gbii, Dowudu etc.) differ (fn. 5: low vs low-mid contrast clearer in Gbii); Hobley 1964 is based on Liberia Inland Mission work between Monrovia and River Cess. Both are Liberian Bassa [bsq] = nucl1418 (not Basaa of Cameroon, Bassa-Nge/Basa of Nigeria, or Bassari).

sources.locator: ch. 3 'Tone', section 3.1, printed p. 20 (p. 23); footnote 4 on printed p. 49 (p. 52). Corroborated by Hobley 1964 JWAL 1(2) p. 51.
sources.note: Whole work is a phonology (chapters: Consonants, Vowels, Tone pp. 20-36, Intonation pp. 37-38, Borrowed Words, Vah script). Ch. 3 opens 'Bassa is a discrete level tone language' (p. 20) with four tonemes (high, mid, low, low-mid) plus consonant-conditioned glides; there is no section or sentence on word stress/accent in Bassa. The word 'stress' occurs only in ch. 5 (pp. 39-42) referring to the stress of ENGLISH source words, which conditions the tone pattern assigned to loans (e.g. p. 41 'Two syllable English words with stress on the first syllable.. are assigned CV́CV̀').

sources.citation: Hobley, June. 1964. A preliminary tonal analysis of the Bassa language. Journal of West African Languages 1(2): 51-55. (Glottolog title 'A preliminary analysis of the Bassa language' omits 'tonal'.)
sources.note: Pike-style tone analysis: 'Bassa is a register-tone language with a slight overlap of contour-tone characteristics' and 'Bassa has three registers, high, mid, and low. Tonemes usually appear on vowels, but they can also appear on syllabic nasals' (p. 51); glides analysed as toneme sequences; tone sandhi. Nothing on stress or accent.

sources.citation: Vogler, Pierre. 2017. Contribution à la classification des langues kru (Niger-Congo). Manuscript deposited in HAL (hal-01574391), 100 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 2.4 (p. 7): Kru tone systems have either three registers (Bassa, Klao, Neyo..) or four (Grebo, Bete, Vata..); the three-register type is taken to be original (contra Marchese Zogbo 2012: 4), the top tone of four-register languages being a local innovation; contour ('modulated') tones combine two or three level tones on one unlengthened vowel, one per mora. Sec. 3.4: in the dewoin-bassa / klao grouping 'le systeme tonal demeure a 3 registres', unlike Nyabwa-Krahn/Guere-Wobe. No statement on stress/accent for Bassa.

tone.quote: standard Niger-Congo features: noun class remnants, verbal extensions, a *CVCV word structure, labio-velars and at least one implosive stop, ATR vowel harmony, nasalized vowels in one half of family, and three to four level tones, as well as common lexical roots ... PROTO-PHONOLOGY ... *Four level tones, with a few examples of 4 > 3, innovated modulated tones resulting from tone-consonant interaction and consonant voicing; tone carries a high functional load in the lexicon and in the grammar: distinguishing 1-2nd person (sg and pl), perfective-imperfective, negation
